item.title: Zero photoemission from icosahedral superatoms
item.description: arXiv:2610.32031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photoemission is expected to occur when the photon energy exceeds the binding energy of an electron, with the photoemission yield generally remaining non-zero above this threshold. Yet, it can be suppressed at specific photon energies, a phenomenon known as the Cooper minimum. Although complete suppression represents an extreme limit of this phenomenon, such zero photoemission has previously been reported only for atoms with an outermost s-type orbital and has never been observed in non-atomic systems. Here, we demonstrate the deliberate realization of zero photoemission from Ag12W-, an artificial icosahedral superatom, by observing a vanishing photoemission cross section 0.85 eV above the detachment threshold and reproducing this behavior in theoretical simulations. These simulations predict that zero photoemission can be common in nearly spherical nanoclusters, a prediction we experimentally confirm using Ag12Mo-, an isoelectronic counterpart of Ag12W-. Because superatoms offer systematic control over both size and elemental composition using the periodic table, our findings establish a route toward active control of photoemission in finite-size quantum systems and stimulate further investigations of underexplored physical phenomena such as nondipole effects.
item.dc:creator: Yuta Suzuki, Mamoru Tanaka, Yoshi-ichi Suzuki, Akira Terasaki, Takuya Horio

item.title: PULSES: multi-agent AI for autonomous excited-state model building and dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.32392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating molecular excited-state processes requires resolving electronic and nuclear dynamics, but the cost of direct quantum-chemical calculations limits accessible system sizes and timescales. Machine-learning models can extend these simulations, yet they often need to be tailored to specific molecular systems and scientific objectives. Building and deploying such models requires coordinated decisions across conformational sampling, quantum-chemical labelling, model training, validation and dynamics. Here we introduce Paired agents for Unified Learning and Simulation of Excited States (PULSES), a multi-agent system that automates this workflow within expert-approved boundaries. A human expert and planner define the scientific objective, methods and decision boundaries, while an orchestrator coordinates domain agents and artifact-specific scientific assurance during execution. We evaluate PULSES on 15 computational chemistry tasks and demonstrate end-to-end applications to perylene exciton Hamiltonians, solvent-dependent biphenyl relaxation, and excited-state proton transfer in 10-hydroxybenzo[h]quinoline. These results demonstrate traceable, expert-bounded construction and deployment of specialized excited-state models, while retaining scientific validation as a requirement rather than assuming that successful execution establishes correctness.
item.dc:creator: Fangning Ren, Lechen Dong, Xu Chen, Weilin Zou, Bushra Alam, Fang Liu

item.title: Quantifying the effect of heavy-atom only augmented basis sets for the calculation of non-covalent interactions
item.description: arXiv:2610.32567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Truncating the basis set is a straightforward way of reducing the computational cost of a calculation, often done by augmenting only the non-hydrogen atoms with diffuse functions. Calculations of non-covalent interactions, which require large diffuse basis sets for quantitative results, regularly employ this truncation. Herein, we assess the validity of this basis set truncation across the A24 and S66 datasets and for case study examples at a range of interaction distances. For the majority of non-covalent interactions, we find that the heavy-atom-only augmented basis sets can be safely applied as a method of reducing computational cost. However, for aliphatic-aliphatic and $\pi$-aliphatic type dispersion interactions, we find that lower cardinal number basis sets with full augmentation for all atoms, including hydrogen, can provide similar or even more accurate results than higher cardinal number basis sets with partial augmentation. These results emphasize that increasing basis set size and computational cost does not necessarily improve accuracy; rather, the composition of a basis set is critical to achieving highly accurate and efficient computations.
item.dc:creator: Stephanie Lambie, Ali Alavi

item.title: Low-variance force estimators for nuclear quantum mean forces
item.description: arXiv:2610.32652v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum equilibrium structure can be sampled using classical molecular dynamics with a learned effective potential for a single path-integral replica, but the primitive mean-force estimates obtained from path-integral molecular dynamics with that replica held fixed are noisy. We derive a scaled-gradient estimator with zero sampling variance for a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator and an estimated 4.7--57.5-fold reduction in constrained-sampling time for the molecular tests. The resulting potentials can be trained on these forces like standard machine-learning interatomic potentials and yield stable production simulations from which quantum expectation values of position-dependent observables are obtained as classical ensemble averages.
item.dc:creator: Venkat Kapil

item.title: Single-molecule cold chemistry: Isotopic branching ratios of the $\mathrm{H_2O^+ + HD}$ reaction at cryogenic temperatures
item.description: arXiv:2610.32904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Isotopic branching in ion-molecule reactions influences interstellar deuterium fractionation, yet its dynamics remain poorly understood for many important systems at astrophysically relevant temperatures. Here, we investigate H- and D-atom transfer in the $\mathrm{H_2O^+ + HD}$ reaction using single sympathetically cooled water ions in a cryogenic radiofrequency trap. Nondestructive identification of the products from 441 individual reaction events at a mean collision energy of 7 K reveals an $\mathrm{H_3O^+/H_2DO^+}$ product branching ratio of $1.50 \pm 0.15$ demonstrating a preferential H-atom transfer. The experiments are rationalized using quasi-classical-trajectory calculations which indicate a transition from direct dynamics at higher energies to a complex-mediated reaction under the present experimental conditions and point to an important role of intramolecular vibrational redistribution affecting the isotopic branching in this regime. The present results extend measurements into an astrochemically relevant energy regime and establish cryogenic single-ion chemistry as a new platform for resolving competing reaction pathways.
item.dc:creator: Nanditha Sunil Kumar, Prerna Paliwal, Mikhail Popov, Xueyi Li, Anyang Li, Hua Guo, Stefan Willitsch

item.title: Nonadiabatic vibrational dynamics of CO on Pt(111) studied with first-principles many-body perturbation theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.31727v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the nonequilibrium vibrational dynamics of CO adsorbed on Pt(111), a prototypical adsorbate-surface system for ultrafast vibrational spectroscopy, using a first-principles framework that combines many-body perturbation theory with density functional theory. Within this methodology we explicitly account for electron-hole pair excitations and electron-mediated phonon-phonon coupling. For the latter mechanism, we evaluate the vertex-correction screening, what constitutes a methodological novelty. Our calculations qualitatively reproduce the transient evolution of the internal stretch vibrational mode observed in femtosecond pump-probe experiments, allowing us to identify in the experimental measurements a small transient blueshift after excitation with a femtosecond laser pulse. As predicted in a previous work, the reduction in the number of electronic states available for electron-phonon coupling when the electronic temperature raises at a group 10 transition metal surface, effectively screens the electron-phonon interaction giving rise to an anomalous transient blue-shift.
item.dc:creator: Ra\'ul Bomb\'in, I\~naki Fern\'andez Tena, J. I\~naki Juaristi, Maite Alducin

item.title: Strontium Titanate Capping Layers as Kinetic Regulators of Redox Phase Transitions in Oxide Heterostructures
item.description: arXiv:2610.31871v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Oxide capping layers are widely used to protect and stabilize thin-film heterostructures, yet their role in governing phase-transition kinetics remains largely unexplored. Here, we uncover the kinetic function of few-nanometer-thick SrTiO$_3$ (STO) capping layers in controlling oxidation and reduction processes, using real-time in situ optical spectroscopic ellipsometry. We show that oxygen diffusion through the nanoscale capping layer constitutes the rate-limiting step, giving rise to diffusion-controlled phase transitions in the underlying materials. As a result, both capping-layer thickness and oxygen partial pressure provide effective handles to tune phase transition temperatures. Quantitative analysis yields an activation energy of $E_A$ = 0.64 $\pm$0.06 eV for oxygen diffusion through STO, highlighting its suitability for precise control of redox reactions in diverse material systems. These results establish oxide capping layers as active kinetic regulators of redox-driven phase transitions and offer a general framework for engineering redox dynamics in complex oxide heterostructures.
item.dc:creator: Pooya Abdollahi, Woo Jin Kim, Keaghan Knight, Harold Y. Hwang, Ambrose Seo

item.title: A classical trajectory method for diatom-atom-atom ternary association reactions
item.description: arXiv:2610.32896v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce a classical trajectory method for calculating direct diatom-atom-atom ternary association re- action rates that incorporates the rotational degrees of freedom of the diatomic reactant. By treating the diatomic molecule as a rigid rotor, we include the effects of the anisotropy of the molecule-atom interaction and the dynamical effects of the rotational motion. We apply this approach to a system of experimental interest, CD+ + He + He, along with the isotopic variant CH+ + He + He -> CHHe+ + He, and examine the role of the internal, rotational degrees of freedom of the diatomic molecule. In particular, we find that in the regime where the collision energy is much smaller than the rotational energy of the entrance channel, the rotational motion leads to deviation from the classical threshold law by violating the assumptions of long-range capture theory models.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Julian, Jesus Perez-Rios

item.title: CO2-Induced Shifts in the Confined Phase Transformation of CH4 in Metal-Organic Frameworks
item.description: arXiv:2610.32918v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A sharp increase in gas uptake over a narrow pressure range can occur for fluids confined in nanoporous materials such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), reflecting a transformation between distinct adsorption states, often accompanied by the existence of metastable states. Understanding how co-adsorbed species modify this behavior is important for predicting and optimizing gas storage and separation. Here, we investigate the effect of CO2 on the adsorption transformation of confined CH4 in rigid IRMOF-1 and IRMOF-8. Transition-Matrix Monte Carlo (TMMC) simulations were performed for systems containing 0-75 and 0-150 CO2 molecules in IRMOF-1 and IRMOF-8, respectively. While the addition of CO2 decreases the maximum CH4 uptake, consistent with competition for pore space, remarkably, the presence of CO2 significantly shifts the discontinuity in the CH4 adsorption isotherm to substantially lower pressures relative to the pure CH4 system. This promotion of the high-density CH4 phase at lower pressures demonstrates that CO2 substantially alters the thermodynamic landscape governing confined CH4 through changes in both fluid-fluid and fluid-framework interactions. These results establish CO2 as a thermodynamic modifier of confined CH4 behavior and suggest that controlled co-adsorption provides a means of tuning adsorption transformations in nanoporous materials.
item.dc:creator: Anthony Dorhauer, Bartosz Mazur, Bogdan Kuchta, Carlos Wexler

item.title: Contrastive Regularization of Machine Learning Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2606.31660v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly trained as regressors and then deployed as generators, from language models to learned simulators. In this setting, accuracy on held-out data says little about the distribution a model produces when it is sampled. We study this problem where the correct distribution is fixed by first principles, in machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) on density functional theory (DFT) energies and forces, then used to run molecular simulations. The MSE never constrains the Boltzmann distribution that the potential defines, so an MLIP can match held-out DFT data and still drift, when sampled, into spurious minima that corrupt its thermodynamics. Building on the variational principle of statistical physics, we introduce Contrastive Regularized MSE (CRMSE), a post-training step in which the potential acts as its own energy-based model and learns to reproduce the distribution it generates, without any new DFT data. On molecules from the MD17 benchmark, CRMSE restores physical sampling and recovers DFT free-energy profiles, while keeping energy and force errors within chemical accuracy. Our results suggest that a model meant to be sampled must be trained on the distribution it produces, not only for pointwise accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Dimitrios Tzivrailis, Georgios Sotiropoulos, Alberto Rosso, Eiji Kawasaki

item.title: Resolving Peak Shifting Effects in Real-Time Time-Dependent Orbital Propagation Methods Through Nonorthogonal Expansions
item.description: arXiv:2608.02931v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-consistent field real-time electronic structure methods are a powerful approach for modeling ultrafast processes but suffer from systematic errors in predicted transition energies, commonly known as peak shifting, that obscure direct comparison with experiment. Although this effect has been explored in single reference methods, a general understanding that extends to multiconfigurational methods remains unresolved. Here, we develop a real-time nonorthogonal multiconfigurational self-consistent field (RT-TD NOMCSCF) formalism in which independently propagated orbital sets generate a compact, nonorthogonal wavefunction. The approach establishes a unified framework for nonlinear real-time electronic structure theories, which we use to reveal the common origin of peak shifting across single and multireference limits. Using this framework, we demonstrate that peak shifting does not arise exclusively from the effect of state averaging over the internal space basis, but also from the accessible external configurational space. By systematically expanding the internal space with independently propagated orbital sets, RT-TD NOMCSCF suppresses this aver- aging, recovers correct transition energies, and distinguishes intrinsic peak shifting from numerical peak drifting caused by propagation errors. Thus, these developments establish nonlinear real-time electronic structure methods that enables more accurate simulations of ultrafast processes.
item.dc:creator: Matheus M. F. de Moraes, Lee M. Thompson

item.title: Derivation of the Sample-Size Scaling of TWO-NN Intrinsic-Dimension Estimates from Molecular Dynamics Trajectories
item.description: arXiv:2609.04914v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The intrinsic dimension of a dataset is the number of independent directions needed to describe the space occupied by its data. Nearest-neighbor estimators infer it from how the probability of finding a neighbor grows around each sampled point. Because the neighbor distances $r$ decrease as the sample grows, the estimated dimension can depend strongly on the number $N$ of available points, which in molecular dynamics is set by trajectory length and saving frequency. We derive the large-sample behavior of the TWO-NN estimator for data drawn from a smooth $d$-dimensional space. The typical nearest-neighbor distance scales as $N^{-1/d}$, and smooth deviations from local uniformity produce corrections in powers of $N^{-2/d}$. Isotropic noise adds a correction proportional to $N^{+2/d}$; for a five-dimensional hyperplane in 100 noisy features, the extended expansion recovers the dimension within a few percent when noise is moderate. We test the scaling on ten independent 100 $\mu$s simulations of alanine dipeptide, represented by the pairwise distances among its ten heavy atoms, whose geometric dimension is $3n_{\mathrm{at}}-6=24$. Over the investigated range, the estimate does not depend systematically on the temporal spacing between configurations, but increases from $7.6$ to $15.6$ as $N$ grows from $10^2$ to $2\times10^5$. Extrapolations that retain corrections through $r^2$, $r^4$, and $r^6$ give limiting dimensions of $24.81$, $23.47$, and $25.30$, respectively. All three estimates lie within 6% of the known dimension and bracket it, and their spread measures the uncertainty due to truncation. The derived scaling provides a practical route from finite-sample estimates to the geometric dimension.
item.dc:creator: Riccardo Capelli

item.title: Convex Analysis of Relaxation Dynamics in Chemical Reaction Networks and Generalized Gradient Flows
item.description: arXiv:2602.18932v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We obtain bounds on the Kullback--Leibler divergence to equilibrium for mass-action chemical reaction networks (CRNs) with equilibrium. The associated trajectory-dependent bounds are characterized in terms of the singular values of the stoichiometric matrix, convexity parameters, and time-integrated activities via deformed-exponential-type functions. We further extend these bounds within a generalized gradient flow framework. We highlight the biological relevance of this framework: the resulting bounds apply to quasi-steady-state regimes, where long transients and plateau-like behavior are common and functionally important. We illustrate the framework using a catalytic CRN exhibiting plateaus, where the bounds provide an a posteriori characterization of slow relaxation induced by local convexity and provide a bound-based approach to quantifying relaxation in CRNs.
item.dc:creator: Keisuke Sugie, Dimitri Loutchko, Tetsuya J. Kobayashi

item.title: Solubility of poorly soluble species in bulk and nanopores from grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.16599v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Poorly soluble species can have mean populations below one in small systems such as nanopores. In this regime, the grand-potential minimum, which identifies the most probable particle number, differs from the ensemble-averaged solute loading. We use grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling (GCWLS) to calculate the density of states $\Omega(N_\mathrm{A}, N_\mathrm{B})$ for a binary Lennard-Jones mixture of solute B in solvent A, both in bulk and in slit pores. One set of GCWLS simulations gives ensemble averages over a range of chemical potentials, whereas conventional grand-canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulation requires a separate simulation at each state point. Independent GCMC simulations confirm the GCWLS ensemble averages. The solvent number distribution is nearly Gaussian, whereas the dilute solute distribution is skewed and Poisson-like. The most probable solute number therefore lies below the ensemble-averaged loading $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle$ and is zero whenever $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle<1$. Reading the solute loading from the grand-potential minimum underestimates it and can falsely indicate that no solute is present. Defining the oversolubility as $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}=x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{conf}}/x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{bulk}}$, where $x_\mathrm{B}$ is the solute mole fraction, we find $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}\approx12$ in a pore of 3.5 particle diameters width when both wall interactions are repulsive. Adding wall-solute attraction moderately raises it to $\approx13$, whereas wall-solvent attraction lowers it to $\approx3.4$. This comparison shows that the wall-solvent interaction controls most of the enhancement. As the pore widens, $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}$ decreases toward unity. In bulk and in nanopores alike, the solubility of poorly soluble species should be obtained from ensemble averages rather than from grand-potential minima.
item.dc:creator: Russell Kajouri, Adyant Agrawal, Philipp St\"ark, Alexander Schlaich, Christian Holm
